beats.say: In 1841 Brunei's sultan secretly negotiated a treaty that let a British trader plant a gunpowder factory on the coast.
The factory, hidden behind the bustling market of Kampong Ayer, supplied explosives to rival Malay sultanates eager to challenge Brunei's dominance.
When the Dutch learned of the covert armament, they dispatched Admiral van den Bosch to demand its demolition.
Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II feigned compliance, but secretly ordered his shipwrights to conceal the gunpowder barrels within the hull of a trading dhow.
During a midnight raid, the Dutch forces found only empty crates, while the hidden barrels detonated later, crippling their flagship.
The explosion forced the Dutch to retreat, granting Brunei a fleeting diplomatic victory that lasted barely a year.
Soon after, British Consul James Brooke capitalized on the chaos, signing a trade pact that gave Britain control over Brunei's lucrative pepper exports.
By 1843 the sultanate's treasury swelled, yet the hidden gunpowder cache remained buried beneath the river's mud, a secret weapon never recovered.
